ety.text: First use appears c. 1903, a modern revival of Old English sibling (“relative, a relation, kinsman”), equivalent to sib + -ling. Compare Middle English siblynges pl, sib, sibbe (“relative; kinsman”), German Sippe. The term apparently meant merely kin or relative until the 20th century when it was applied in a way that aided the study of genetics, which led to its specialized use. For example, the OED has a citation in 1902 in which sibling must be defined for those who do not know the intended meaning.

senses.d: A person who shares a parent; one's brother or sister who one shares a parent with.
ex: None of my siblings are married yet.
She also had one sibling, her younger brother Joshua, who was born a year after her.

senses.d: A node in a data structure that shares its parent with another node.
The most closely related species, or one of several most closely related species when none can be determined to be more closely related.
ex: Bush suggested that this difference might represent a case of chromosomal polymorphism or, more likely, sibling species.

grp.label: person who shares same parents — see also brother, sister

ety.text: Learned borrowing from Latin frātria, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek φρᾱτρίᾱ (phrātríā), from φρᾱ́τηρ (phrā́tēr) + -ίᾱ (-íā). Doublet of frairie (see also confrérie).
From Latin frātellus, a diminutive of Latin frāter, from Proto-Italic *frātēr, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr.
From Latin soror, from a diminutive form or based on the model of fratello. Ultimately from Proto-Italic *swezōr, from Proto-Indo-European *swésōr.
Inherited from Old Spanish ermano, from Vulgar Latin *germānus (“brother”), from Latin germānus (“of a brother or sister”). Compare English germane. Displaced Old Spanish fradre, from fratēr.
Inherited from Old Spanish ermana, from Latin germāna.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese irmão (“brother”), from Latin germānus (“brother”), from the adjective germānus (“of true siblings”), from germen (“sprout, bud”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénh₁mn̥ (“offspring, seed”), from *ǵenh₁- (“to beget, to give birth”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese irmãa, yrmãa, from Latin germāna (“sister”), from the adjective germānus (“of siblings”); more at irmão. By surface analysis, irmão + -a (forms feminine equivalents).
